planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Leavenworth's sedge is a fine-textured Gulf South native increasingly sold as a shade lawn substitute, spacing 6-12 inches apart for a solid groundcover within a couple of seasons.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Leavenworth's sedge is a fine, soft-textured native sedge of the Gulf South and lower Midwest, forming a low, arching, bright-green tuft that has become one of the go-to native lawn substitutes for shaded areas under oaks and other large trees where turfgrass struggles. It tolerates occasional mowing on the highest setting for a more lawn-like look, or can be left unmowed for a softer, naturalistic texture. More sun-tolerant than many shade sedges, it also performs well in dappled or morning-sun sites. It spreads gradually by both self-seeding and short rhizomes to fill in as a dense, low-maintenance groundcover that needs no fertilizer or irrigation once established, and it tolerates the periodic dry spells common in Gulf South summers better than cool-season lawn grasses growing in shade.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana sedge grows naturally at the shaded margins of Gulf Coast swamps, bottomland woods, and pond edges and needs reliable moisture to perform well.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Louisiana sedge is a Gulf Coast native of shaded bottomland woods, swamp margins, and pond edges, forming arching clumps of medium-textured green foliage well suited to the wet-shade conditions that stump many other groundcovers. It is a good choice for the shaded, poorly drained corner of a yard, the margin of a rain garden basin under tree canopy, or the damp ground beside a pond or stream where standing water is common after rain. Established clumps spread slowly and need little care beyond adequate moisture; they tolerate occasional flooding without harm. Like other native sedges, it provides structure and habitat value with none of the maintenance demands of a mowed lawn, and it combines well with ferns and other wet-shade natives in a naturalistic planting.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade; giant sedge forms much larger, bolder clumps than most native sedges and needs reliable moisture, growing naturally in southeastern bottomland swamps and wet woods.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; giant sedge is a bold, architectural southeastern native, forming substantial arching clumps of broad, glossy, deep-green blades noticeably larger in scale than the fine-textured sedges typically used as lawn substitutes. It grows naturally in bottomland swamps and wet woods across the Gulf South and makes a strong structural accent or specimen clump at the edge of a pond, rain garden, or shaded wet spot, contrasting well with finer-textured ferns and grasses nearby. It needs consistently moist to wet soil to reach its full size and tolerates periodic flooding without issue. Established clumps require little maintenance beyond adequate moisture; cut back old foliage in late winter if it becomes tattered before new growth emerges in spring.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full to partial shade; long sedge grows naturally in wet woods, seeps, and bog margins and is valued as much for its unusual inflated seed heads as for its foliage.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; long sedge is a native wetland woodland sedge grown as much for its distinctive seed heads as for its arching, medium-green foliage — in summer it produces unusually large, inflated, spiky seed capsules clustered along the flowering stems, giving it a coarser, more textural presence than most fine-leaved sedges and making it a conversation piece in a shaded rain garden or bog planting. It grows naturally in wet woods, seeps, and bog margins and needs reliably moist to wet, acidic soil to perform well, tolerating standing water for extended periods. A good choice for the consistently damp, shaded low spot in a rain garden where turf and most perennials struggle. Established clumps need little care beyond adequate moisture.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in moist, fertile, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; limestone meadow sedge tolerates a wider range of light and moisture conditions than many sedges, from wet meadows to average garden soil.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil, tolerant of neutral to alkaline conditions, in partial shade to full sun; limestone meadow sedge is an easy-care native with attractive blue-green foliage, naturally found in wet meadows, moist woodland edges, and floodplains across much of the eastern and central US. It is more adaptable than many sedges, handling everything from consistently moist meadow soil to average garden conditions and tolerating both more sun and more shade than fussier species, which has made it a popular, forgiving choice at native plant nurseries for rain gardens, meadow plantings, and naturalistic borders. It spreads gradually to form a soft, low-textured groundcover and combines well with other native perennials in a mixed planting. Established clumps need little maintenance beyond routine moisture during dry spells.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white edge sedge is a graceful native woodland sedge that tolerates both drier upland shade and consistently moist woodland soil.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white edge sedge is a graceful eastern woodland native with slender, arching foliage and delicate, drooping flower spikes in late spring that give the plant a soft, airy texture distinct from the stiffer, more upright habit of many other sedges. Growing naturally in deciduous forest understory across a range of moisture conditions, from drier upland woods to moist bottomland, it adapts well to typical shade garden soil without demanding consistently wet ground. It combines nicely with ferns, wildflowers, and other native shade perennials, adding fine textural contrast to bolder-leaved companions. Established plants need little maintenance beyond routine watering during extended dry spells; leave old foliage in place over winter and tidy up in early spring before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full to partial shade; brome-like sedge grows naturally in wooded swamps and wet depressions and is useful for stabilizing consistently soggy, shaded ground.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; brome-like sedge is a native wetland woodland sedge with fine, grass-like, arching foliage forming loose tufts, naturally found in wooded swamps, seasonally flooded depressions, and the muddy margins of woodland streams. It tolerates standing water for extended periods and thrives in the kind of consistently soggy, shaded ground where lawn grass and many perennials fail outright, making it useful for stabilizing soil at the edge of a rain garden basin, drainage swale, or low spot in a wooded yard. Established plantings spread modestly and need little care beyond reliable moisture. It provides valuable habitat and forage for wetland wildlife while requiring no fertilizer, mowing, or other routine maintenance once settled.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade; cattail sedge grows naturally in bottomland woods and along pond and stream margins and is named for its distinctive thick, cattail-like seed spikes.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; cattail sedge is a distinctive native of bottomland woods, pond margins, and shaded stream edges, named for its thick, cylindrical seed spikes that resemble a miniature cattail flower head — an unusual and easily identifiable feature among native sedges. The arching, medium-green foliage forms a loose clump that fits naturally at the shaded edge of a pond or rain garden alongside true cattails, sedges, and other wetland natives. It tolerates periodic flooding and needs consistently moist to wet soil to perform its best, making it a poor choice for a typical dry border but a strong one for a shaded water's-edge planting. Established clumps require little maintenance beyond reliable moisture.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant plugs in spring in lean, dry, well-drained, poor soil in full sun to partial shade; poverty oatgrass is adapted to nutrient-poor ground and is increasingly used in no-mow native lawn and meadow plantings, tolerating conditions too poor for most turf grasses.

directions: Plant in lean, dry, poor, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; poverty oatgrass is a tough, low-growing native bunchgrass named for its ability to thrive on nutrient-poor, sandy, or rocky ground where few other grasses persist, forming neat, dense tufts of fine, semi-evergreen foliage that stays attractive through much of the year. It has drawn growing interest for no-mow native lawn alternatives and low-input meadow plantings, since it needs no fertilizer, tolerates drought once established, and stays naturally low without regular mowing. It is also an important larval host plant for several native skipper butterflies, adding ecological value beyond its low-maintenance appeal. Because it is adapted to lean soil, avoid rich, heavily amended garden beds, which encourage floppy growth at the expense of its naturally tidy, resilient habit; the poorer the site, the better it tends to perform.
sources: Xerces Society — Native Plant and Pollinator Resources

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; three-flower melic grass is an under-planted southeastern woodland native, a good alternative to the more commonly grown Chasmanthium (inland sea oats) for a shaded grass with less self-seeding vigor.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; three-flower melic grass is a graceful, under-planted native woodland bunchgrass, producing soft mounds of fine green foliage topped in late spring by open, airy flower panicles with distinctive drooping, oat-like spikelets that catch light beautifully in dappled shade. It offers a similar naturalistic, woodland-grass look to the more widely planted inland sea oats (Chasmanthium latifolium) but with a noticeably more restrained, clump-forming habit and far less aggressive self-seeding, making it a better-behaved choice for a smaller or more formal shade garden bed where self-sown seedlings would be unwelcome. It goes dormant and dies back by mid-summer in its native range, so plan companion plantings to carry interest through the second half of the growing season. Established clumps need little care beyond routine moisture and a spring cleanup of old foliage.
